Stationary increments

OUP_StationaryIncrements.Rd

Stationary increments are created from pseudo-random standard normal variables generated by four random number generators.

Format

csv file with 1001 rows and 5 columns

Details

  • tau: time variable

  • dqrng: dqrng::pcg64 uniform random numbers with Ziggurat transform to normal

  • mt19937: std::mt19937 uniform random numbers with Polar Box-Muller transform to normal

  • sitmo: sitmo::prng uniform random numbers with Polar Box-Muller transform to normal

  • rnorm: rnorm uniform random numbers with cumulative normal inversion

An important assumption of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Process is stationary increments. An increment is eps(t-s)^0.5, where eps~N(0,1) and t-s is a time interval. This data has time intervals equal to one and eps from dqrng, an optional package, mt19937, the generator in c++, sitmo, an optional package, and rnorm, the default generator in R.

Random number generators must pass many tests. Here we test for stationary increments as a special case of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Process. The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Process is stationary if rho goes to infinity and sigma goes to infinity in such a way that sigma/(2rho)^0.5 goes to a constant.

To conduct a test, first estimate the unrestricted parameters. With time intervals equal to one, parameter rho equal to 3 or more is closer to infinity than to zero. Then impose restrictions. Choose a large number with an easy square root, such as 1600. Set 2rho=1600, or rho=800. Set mu=0. Set sigma=40, which is the square root of 1600 and imposes the restriction that sigma/(2rho)^0.5=1.

Then do a Likelihood Ratio Test comparing the unrestricted and restricted estimates. If the Log Likelihoods are not significantly different, the hypothesis of stationary increments cannot be rejected.
